paras: The threatened lynching of George Mack took place in Huntingdon, Pennsylvania, in August 1885, after Mack, a Black circus worker some papers called Mock, was jailed on a charge of joining in an assault on a girl near the grounds of Cole's circus on August 10. Dispatches reported "strong talk" and "wild talk" of lynching him, and a later wire said mob violence was "loudly threatened" against him and a second accused man in the same jail. No attack was reported, and by late August Mack was awaiting trial.

Cole's circus exhibited at Huntingdon on Monday, August 10, 1885, and its train was to leave for Bedford that night. According to a Huntingdon dispatch printed in the Altoona Tribune, a young man named Kemberling, alias "Fatty," of Altoona, lured Bertha Morrison, 17, of Centre Union, away from the crowd; the wire called her Flora.

The dispatch said eleven other circus attachés, two of them Black, seized and gagged her and assaulted her in the woods. A neighbor, named variously as John McCahan, McKeown and McCohen, came to her aid and was then beaten unconscious, by two Black men lying in wait according to the specials, or by a single "powerful colored man" according to the New-York Tribune.

Police searched the departing circus train and arrested one man, George Mack, who was reported found hidden in a carriage or under the steam calliope's canvas. On August 11 he was arraigned before Justice Murray and remanded to jail, several reports saying the girl identified him. The Huntingdon specials that day reported "every indication of a lynching to-night" and "Wild talk ... on all sides of lynching Mack."

Kimberlin, accused as the principal, was arrested in Altoona on August 12 and lodged in the Huntingdon jail. A United Press dispatch then reported "extra precautions" to shield the two prisoners from mob violence "which is loudly threatened," and the Washington Evening Star said Kimberlin was "threatened with lynching." No report of a crowd gathering at the jail appears in the coverage.

On August 14 Policeman Decker overtook the circus at Meyersdale and arrested an umbrella seller who gave his name as Henry Wilson. A Huntingdon special of August 23 listed Kimberling and George Mack among the principal prisoners in a jail "guarded by a strong force of watchmen," and a Juniata County paper noted "quiet excitement" and a September trial. In early September Kemberling named accomplices, and Samuel Stair of Smithfield was arrested. No report of the trial or its outcome appears in the coverage.

The first wire account, carried by the Washington Evening Star, the Indianapolis Journal, the Memphis Daily Appeal and others, described "Ten white men and a negro named George Mack" and did not mention lynching. The St. Paul Daily Globe nonetheless printed that text under the headline "Judge Lynch Wanted." The Huntingdon specials in the Sun, the Morning Journal and Courier and the Altoona Tribune called the crime a "fiendish outrage" by "inhuman monsters," while the New-York Tribune headlined its version "Beaten with a Club by a Negro."

The United Press follow-up on Kimberlin ran as "Another Miscreant Captured" in the Rock Island Argus and as "Torture Him to Death" in the Maysville Daily Evening Bulletin. None of these white papers commented on the lynching talk, which they reported as part of the news of the crime. The Cleveland Gazette, in a "Notes and Comments" column that also covered an A. M. E. pastor and a Black man shot by a Kentucky deputy marshal, condensed the story to four sentences ending "a lynching is imminent," without comment.

The Sun, the Morning Journal and Courier and the Cleveland Gazette called the accused man Mock, while the wire, the Altoona Tribune dispatch and the later court lists called him Mack. The wire counted one Black man among eleven attackers, the specials two among twelve. The Altoona dispatch said the girl and two eyewitnesses, George Ream and Lincoln Corbin, identified Mack, whereas the New-York Tribune said neither she nor McCahan could positively identify him and that a witness at the hearing placed him among the men.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of George Mack in Huntingdon, Pennsylvania
bases: Dispatches reported talk and threats of lynching George Mack, a Black circus worker jailed on an assault charge, and of mob violence against him and a co-accused in the Huntingdon jail; no attack was reported (A3, A18, A11).

No one was killed: Mack was reported still in jail awaiting the September court term (A20, A22); the episode is a threatened lynching, with lynching talk and threats of mob violence reported (A3, A18, A11) but no crowd or attempt.

Independent dispatches (the AP wire A1, the Huntingdon specials A2/A3/A17-A18, the New-York Tribune special A4 and the United Press wire A11) agree that Mack was arrested and jailed, and the specials and the UP wire separately report lynching talk or threats (A3, A18, A11, A14).

framing.detail: The AP-type wire ran widely under headlines such as 'Brutal Outrage Upon a Young Girl' and, in St. Paul, 'Judge Lynch Wanted.'
The Huntingdon specials described a 'fiendish outrage' by 'inhuman monsters' and reported the lynching talk as news without criticism.
The New-York Tribune headlined 'Beaten with a Club by a Negro' but reported doubts about the identification.
The UP follow-up on Kimberlin ran as 'Another Miscreant Captured' and, in Maysville, 'Torture Him to Death.'
The Cleveland Gazette (indexed as white press) ran a four-sentence summary in 'Notes and Comments' with no comment on the lynching threat.

info: Assault alleged on the night of Monday, August 10, 1885; Mack arrested that night; lynching talk reported August 11-14.
Near the circus grounds at Huntingdon, in a lonely spot in Walker township per the Altoona Tribune dispatch; Mack held in the Huntingdon county jail.
George Mack (also printed Mock), described as 'colored' and a circus employee, threatened with lynching; a co-accused, Kimberlin/Kemberling, was also reported threatened.
Accused of taking part in an assault ('outrage') by circus attachés on Bertha (or Flora) Morrison, 17, of Centre Union, and of beating her rescuer.
Unnamed townspeople; dispatches report 'talk' of lynching and that mob violence was 'loudly threatened'; no mob is reported to have formed.
Mack remained in jail awaiting trial as of late August; no lynching reported.
